## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="w9-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Power and energy</dt><dd>A 25 MW, 100 MWh battery charges or discharges at up to 25 MW and holds up to 100 MWh: four hours flat out.</dd>
<dt>Round-trip efficiency</dt><dd>This battery returns 80% of what goes in; the rest becomes heat.</dd>
<dt>State of charge</dt><dd>The energy stored at the end of each hour; it links each hour to the next.</dd>
<dt>Value</dt><dd>The battery's value is what it saves the town: $7,240 on this day with the best schedule.</dd>
<dt>Decisions</dt><dd>For each hour: how much the battery charges and discharges, and how much it then holds.</dd>
<dt>Goal</dt><dd>The lowest running cost for the town's day.</dd>
<dt>Rules</dt><dd>At most 25 MW in or out; 0 to 100 MWh stored; 80% of what goes in is stored; supply equals demand every hour.</dd>
</dl>
<table class="lx-facts">
<caption>Four 25 MW batteries on 9 June 2025, each with its best schedule</caption>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Battery</th><th scope="col">Saving that day</th><th scope="col">Per MWh of storage</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>1 hour, 25 MWh</td><td class="n">$2,500</td><td class="n">$100</td></tr>
<tr><td>2 hours, 50 MWh</td><td class="n">$5,000</td><td class="n">$100</td></tr>
<tr><td>4 hours, 100 MWh</td><td class="n">$7,240</td><td class="n">$72</td></tr>
<tr><td>8 hours, 200 MWh</td><td class="n">$7,336</td><td class="n">$37</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Prices, losses and the break-even spread</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Break-even.** A MWh stored at price $p_\text{in}$ comes back as 0.8 MWh, so it pays only if the selling price beats $p_\text{in}/0.8$: buy at \$40, sell above \$50.
- **Spilled sun.** It costs \$0, so storing it always passes that test.
- **One more MWh.** Each hour's [price]{.lx-term term="marginal-cost"} is the cost of one more MWh. A 25 MW battery is more than that: at 08:00 only 3 MW of sun is spilled, so full-power charging takes 22 MW from gas at \$40.
- **The real saving.** So this lesson counts what the town actually saves. Your best full-power schedule saves \$6,360; the solver saves \$7,240 by charging at part power, matching each hour's spill.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The battery's day as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Decisions for each hour $t$: charging, discharging and the [state of charge]{.lx-term term="state-of-charge"}, with the gas plants and spill as in lesson 0.

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $t$ | the hour, 0 to 23 (1 MW for one hour = 1 MWh) | – |
| $p_{\mathrm{cc},t}$, $p_{\mathrm{pk},t}$ | combined-cycle and peaker output | MW |
| $s_t$ | spilled wind and sun | MW |
| $c_t$, $d_t$ | battery charging and discharging | MW |
| $e_t$ | energy stored at the end of hour $t$ | MWh |
| $g_t$ | the gap: demand minus nuclear, wind and sun | MW |
| $w_t$, $\sigma_t$ | wind and sun output | MW |

$$\min \sum_t \big(40\,p_{\mathrm{cc},t} + 100\,p_{\mathrm{pk},t}\big)$$

Rules for every hour, top to bottom: balance, state of charge, power, energy, the gas plants' sizes and spill.

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{\mathrm{cc},t} + p_{\mathrm{pk},t} - s_t + d_t - c_t = g_t\\
e_t = e_{t-1} + 0.8\,c_t - d_t, \quad e_{-1} = 0\\
0 \le c_t,\ d_t \le 25\\
0 \le e_t \le 100\\
0 \le p_{\mathrm{cc},t} \le 150, \quad 0 \le p_{\mathrm{pk},t} \le 100\\
0 \le s_t \le w_t + \sigma_t
\end{gathered}
$$

- **Over time.** The state-of-charge rule is the only one linking one hour to the next; it makes storage a problem over time.
- **Losses.** Here the whole loss sits on charging; many models split it, $\sqrt{0.8}$ each way.
- **Left out of the goal.** The nuclear plant's \$24,000 for the day is the same in every plan.
- **Always an answer.** The page's code also allows unserved demand at \$3,000/MWh, so the model always has a solution; on this day none is needed.
- **Next.** [Lesson 10](10-write-it-down.qmd) writes such a model down and [lesson 11](11-solver.qmd) checks a solver's answer. [M3](m03-capacity-expansion.qmd) (capacity expansion) chooses the battery's size too, and A8 (how long should storage last?, upcoming) will.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>One day only. A battery's yearly value needs every day of the year, including days with no spilled sun (lesson A8, upcoming).</li>
<li>Perfect foresight: the solver knows the whole day in advance. Real operators schedule with forecasts that miss (lesson 4).</li>
<li>The cost of building the battery and of its wear, which would set a minimum spread worth cycling for (lesson 7).</li>
<li>The combined-cycle's ramp limit from lesson 0, and any limit on the wires.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="w9-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mw" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A battery's MWh rating tells you its maximum power.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The MWh say how much it holds; a separate MW rating says how fast. Prairie Town's 100 MWh battery delivers at most 25 MW, for four hours.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="make" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A battery adds energy to the grid.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It moves energy in time and loses some on the way: this one returns 80% of what goes in.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spread" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Buying at $40/MWh and selling at $45/MWh pays for this battery.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. 1 MWh bought for $40 returns 0.8 MWh, worth $36 at $45. It needs a selling price above $50.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="w9">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="earn" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 50 MW, 200 MWh battery with 80% round trip charges 100 MWh at $20/MWh and later sells all it stored at $60/MWh. What does it earn?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$4,000</li><li data-value="b">$2,800</li><li data-value="c">$4,800</li><li data-value="d">$2,000</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$2,800: it stores 80 MWh and sells them for 80 × $60 = $4,800, minus the $2,000 it paid.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dur" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">On 9 June 2025, going from a 4-hour to an 8-hour battery (both 25 MW) raises Prairie Town's saving by how much?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">It doubles</li><li data-value="b">About half again</li><li data-value="c">Only $96</li><li data-value="d">Nothing at all</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Only $96 ($7,240 to $7,336): it stores the last 3 MWh of spilled sun and returns 2.4 MWh at $40. The peaker's last 5 MWh remain, since both discharge at most 25 MW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
